title: The colors
hook: sunsets redden because light crosses more air and the blues scatter away

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was solstice, when the sun seems to stand still. Your line was it moves: the sunset point walks the horizon all year.

At noon, the sky is blue and the sun is a hard white. In the last hour before dark, everything goes gold. Then orange, then pink, sometimes a red so deep it looks painted, and after the sun is gone, a soft blue-violet that seems to glow from nowhere. Same sun. Same sky. Same air. So where do the colors come from, and why only now? A child might ask it. Scientists asked it too, and the answer took them until the eighteen hundreds.

Sunlight looks white, but it's every color mixed together, as a rainbow shows. Passing through the air, it bumps into molecules far too small to see, and they scatter some of it in every direction. The key: they scatter the short, blue wavelengths much more than the long, red ones. In the eighteen sixties the Irish physicist John Tyndall studied this in the lab, and in 1871 the English physicist Lord Rayleigh worked out the math. It's called Rayleigh scattering. At noon, the sun is high, and its light takes a short path through the air. Blue gets scattered all over the sky, which is why the sky looks blue. At sunset, the sun is low, and its light slants through many times as much air to reach you. Along that long road, most of the blue is scattered off to the side. What arrives at your eyes is the long-wave light: yellow, orange, red. Dust, smoke and tiny droplets can deepen it. After the volcano Krakatoa erupted in 1883, its ash and gases spread high around the world, and people as far away as Europe and North America saw sunsets so fiery that some thought there was a fire in the distance. And after the sun disappears, clouds high up can still catch its light, blushing pink while the ground goes gray. Knowing the physics takes nothing from the view. Tonight's orange is sunlight that slanted through a long road of air, and lost its blue on the way to you.
screen: `WHITE LIGHT IS EVERY COLOR.` · `BLUE SCATTERS MOST.` · `A LONG ROAD THROUGH THE AIR.` · `KRAKATOA'S FIERY SKIES.` · then, large: `THREE COLORS.`

segments.voice: Look slowly around the room you're in and find three colors, not just blue or white but the exact shade: the gray-green of a plant, the honey of a wooden table, the pale pink of a hand. Name each one inside. Tonight's sky can get the same close look.
The colors. Sunsets redden because the low sun's light crosses more air, and the blues scatter away. Today's word.
Your line: three colors. Same sun, same sky, a longer road of air. Day one hundred fifty, done.

howItsDone: Painters, photographers and sky watchers study sunset colors closely, and physics classes explain them with Rayleigh scattering: blue light scatters more, so a low sun looks orange and red.

fork.setup: the sun is low, and its light slants through far more air than at noon. what happens to the blue?
fork.reveal: most of the blue is scattered off to the side along the long road. what reaches your eyes is yellow, orange and red.

trapdoor: what you thought: sunsets are red because the sun cools down at night.
what it means: the low sun's light crosses more air, and the blues scatter away, leaving the reds.
what a scholar hears: Rayleigh scattering (1871), strongly favoring short wavelengths; Tyndall's earlier experiments; the 1883 Krakatoa sunsets.

sources.ref: Lord Rayleigh (J. W. Strutt), On the light from the sky, its polarization and colour, Philosophical Magazine (1871)

notes: Rayleigh 1871 and Tyndall's 1860s experiments: confirm dates and nationalities (Tyndall Irish; Rayleigh English).
